accuracy.evidence: Checked against the EYFS statutory framework ELG Building Relationships (work and play cooperatively, take turns, form friendships with peers), the Development Matters 3-4 example about accepting that not everyone can be Spider-Man and suggesting other ideas, and the Head Start ELOF preschool goals on positive interactions and cooperative play. The watch-then-offer-a-fitting-idea sequence and the warning against changing the game follow the group-entry findings of Putallaz and Gottman and Corsaro's access rituals.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented group-entry slips: barging in or grabbing (watch-first prediction and clue hunt), drawing attention to yourself with Me! Me! (ask sort), redirecting the group to a new game such as football or TV (idea step feedback), silent hovering (Hide and say nothing card), and reading not now as never or they hate me (not-now prediction and the never and hate challenge tags).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagentry is built around joining a group already at play: a shop scene where only the apples, coins and basket reveal the game, a gap in three different games (shops, pirate ship, den) that only a role fitting that game can fill, and a mood face that recovers only through calm next steps. No other flagship lab models entering an ongoing game, and the 30 percent shingle gate passed against every lab, including flagplay and flagask.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers that the scene itself tells you the game before Bo asks, then sees that football or bossing is refused while the shopper, parrot and blanket roles are welcomed, so fitting the game is learned by trying. The mood face only lifts with calm choices, and the order step rebuilds watch, ask, give an idea, play from the cards.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: run in and grab a toy versus watch first, Let's play football versus I can be the shopper for a game of shops, and whether not now means never. The clue hunt, the refused football card and the Bo-feels-OK ending each disprove the wrong option before the done message echoes it back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with nine tagged wrong-answer messages (grab, loud, push, quiet, newgame, boss, spoil, never, hate). Each names the slip, for example tag is a new game so give an idea for their doctors game, or not now does not mean they do not like you because the game may be full.

readability.evidence: Family audience gates pass: the kid paragraphs use short sentences and words such as watch, kind words, idea and not now, well under the FK 5.0 target; the adult paragraphs keep the curriculum terms Building Relationships, cooperative play and group entry while scoring about FK 7.9 against the 10.0 limit.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and explanation overlap under the 12 percent limit, including against Playing alongside and together and Sharing and taking turns. Every adult paragraph carries a curriculum reference, a research finding, named mistakes or what the lab does, and item explanations give the reason rather than repeating the answer.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop. Screenshots at 390 px in light and dark themes show the clue emojis, idea cards and calm cards as big tap targets; long idea and calm labels wrap onto two lines instead of being squashed, and every drag has a full-width button twin below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with every spoken message, every tap or drag has a labelled button (for example Look at the coins, or Say I can be the shopper), canvas text uses dark ink on pale tiles in light mode and light ink on slate in dark mode, and reduced motion shortens the auto-play delays.
